name: Title
text:
Chest X-Ray Image Retrieval
Under Declining Target-Pathology Prevalence

name: Authors
text: Presented by Ofei Obuobisah Bekoe

name: Affiliation
text:
Department of Computer Science & Engineering
University of Mines and Technology, Tarkwa, Ghana

Presenting on behalf of the study authors: Obed Appiah, Ezekiel Mensah Martey, Emmanuel Asante, Ernest Kwame Ampomah, Ofei Obuobisah Bekoe, Henry Cobbinah, Boateng Kwedwo Amponsah and Grace Tsomemanya Tulasi. Obed Appiah is affiliated with the University of Energy and Natural Resources, Ghana; the remaining authors are affiliated with the University of Mines and Technology, Ghana. The presenter identity and contact follow the supplied ICAST template. Introduce the distinction between gallery prevalence and training-set imbalance.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: When relevant cases become rare

name: Question
text:
How much retrieval quality do we lose
when relevant cases become rarer?

name: Context
text: The query stays the same. The gallery still contains 20,000 images.

name: Start label
text: Relevant cases at 5% prevalence

name: End label
text: Relevant cases at 0.5% prevalence

name: Evidence note
text: A fixed-gallery benchmark can miss this tenfold reduction in relevant-case availability.

Content-based medical image retrieval returns reference images ranked by visual representation similarity. Potential uses include case-based education and second-opinion reference. The present experiment holds the fitted model, query set and total gallery size fixed. Only the selected target share decreases, with other pathology distractor quotas fixed and background filling the remaining positions. This is evaluation-time prevalence variation, not a change in training-data balance.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: Research gap and study questions

name: Prior heading
text: Prior retrieval evaluations

name: Prior explanation
text:
Pretrained embeddings, rare diseases
and imbalanced galleries already
have substantial literature.

name: Protocol distinction
text:
Changing examples per class in a
balanced index changes support
while preserving relative prevalence.

name: Questions heading
text: This controlled experiment

name: Question one
text:
1  How does declining target prevalence
    affect retrieval across pathologies
    and representation models?

name: Question two
text:
2  From the same SwAV initialization,
    does contrastive adaptation improve
    retrieval over classification?

name: Evidence note
text: The comparison concerns six ResNet-50 conditions and three target pathologies.

The narrative review found no controlled multi-level reduction in target prevalence with query sets and fitted representations held fixed among the reviewed studies. This does not imply that scarcity has been ignored. Denner et al. [1] provide a close conceptual precedent but vary balanced index support, so their reported retrieval metrics are not numerically comparable. The study does not establish a universal ordering of supervised and self-supervised learning.

name: Text 1
text: Data sources and experimental roles

alt: Original manuscript data-flow figure showing NIH, SIIM, common-class sources, deduplication, patient separation and the tuberculosis audit.

text:
Figure 1 from the supplied manuscript, with only the redundant figure title cropped. NIH ChestX-ray14 supplied multi-label adaptation data, cardiomegaly and emphysema queries, and retrieval-pool images after patient exclusions. SIIM supplied pneumothorax queries. External sources supplied normal, pneumonia and COVID-19 adaptation data. Target-positive NIH patients were excluded from adaptation and background partitions. NIH adaptation splits contained 48,280 training, 12,266 validation and 10,620 background images. The common-class dataset contained 4,545 images after source-class balancing, split 80:20. External metadata did not establish exhaustive finding labels or full patient identity. The tuberculosis audit excluded TB as an evaluated target, while retaining it as a fixed 2% distractor.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

title: A fixed gallery with declining prevalence

name: Fixed heading

name: Fixed variables
text:

The fitted model and retrieval depth

name: Replication
text: 3 targets × 4 prevalence levels × 5 gallery samples

name: Evidence note
text: 60 galleries. All six models use identical gallery manifests and fixed query sets.

Targets are cardiomegaly, emphysema and pneumothorax. Each gallery has the selected target count, 400 images from each of three non-target pathologies, and background images filling remaining positions. TB remains one distractor. Cardiomegaly and emphysema use at most one NIH query per patient and exclude query patients from NIH retrieval pools. Pneumothorax uses SIIM queries and an NIH relevant pool. Five gallery seeds resample image identities under source quotas. All fitted models use the same manifests. The five samples estimate gallery-sampling sensitivity, not training variability.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: Six representation conditions

name: Evidence note
text: Shared ResNet-50 backbone. Target labels are absent from available fine-tuning annotations.

All conditions provide 2,048-dimensional global average-pooled embeddings after removing the classification layer. CNN-PT and SwAV-PT use ImageNet-pretrained representations without task adaptation. CNN-Common uses the balanced external common-class data. CNN-NIH, SwAV-CLS and SwAV-SupCon share NIH partitions. The SwAV checkpoint is the official 800-epoch ImageNet model. Held out and zero-shot refer to available fine-tuning labels, not verified clinical absence of target pathology in every image.

name: Text 1
text: Adaptation and exact image retrieval

name: Learning heading
text: Contrastive adaptation

name: Learning text
text:
Two augmented views of each image

Positive-pair weights follow the
overlap of NIH label sets

Projection head supports training
and is removed for retrieval

name: Retrieval heading
text: Retrieval for every condition

name: Retrieval text
text:
1  Resize and normalize the image

2  Extract a 2,048-D embedding

3  Apply L2 normalization

4  Rank the full gallery by cosine similarity

name: Evidence note
text: AdamW, learning rate 0.0001. One fitted checkpoint per learned condition.

Training uses grayscale replicated over three channels and 224 × 224 resizing, ImageNet normalization, horizontal flips, rotation, crops and brightness/contrast jitter. Evaluation uses resizing and normalization only. AdamW learning rate and weight decay are 1e-4, cosine annealing over at most 50 epochs, and early stopping after at least ten epochs with patience seven. Classification uses 64 images per batch. SupCon uses 64 source images with two views, 128 views per step, a 2,048-2,048-128 projection head and temperature 0.07. Distinct-image positive weights are Jaccard overlaps of NIH label sets; the paired view of the same image has weight one. Objective-specific validation losses select checkpoints. Exact ranking uses normalized dot products, equivalent to cosine similarity. Query images are excluded. Training ran on two Tesla T4 GPUs with PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128.

name: Text 1
text: Retrieval metrics and statistical tests

name: Precision label
text: Precision@10

name: Precision meaning
text:
Relevant results among the first ten,
divided by ten.

name: Ndcg label
text: nDCG@10

name: Ndcg meaning
text:
Adds sensitivity to where relevant
images appear in the top ten.

name: Inference label
text: Paired comparisons

name: Inference meaning
text:
Average each query across five galleries.

Use paired Wilcoxon tests and
global Holm correction.

Bootstrap intervals describe uncertainty
conditional on the observed galleries.

name: Evidence note
text: Primary contrast: 5% versus 0.5%. Error bars across galleries do not measure retraining variability.

P@10 is the primary endpoint; nDCG@10 checks ranking position. Relevance is binary and label-based for the designated query pathology. Each gallery has at least 100 relevant images, so the ideal top ten are all relevant. Prevalence effects use Friedman tests and Kendall W, followed by the primary paired contrast. Holm families contain 18 prevalence contrasts per metric. Six planned model comparisons over three pathologies and four prevalence levels give 72 globally corrected comparisons. Unadjusted 95% percentile intervals use 10,000 paired query resamples and are not simultaneous intervals. Statistical significance follows adjusted p-values.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: Every model loses precision

name: Loss description
text:
Relative P@10 reduction across all 18 pairs.
Every decline survives Holm correction.

All P@10 endpoint means are copied from manuscript Table 2. The highlighted SupCon row has the highest mean at both endpoints for each target and also ranks first at 1% and 2%. Relative reductions range from 83.4% to 91.9% across the 18 model-pathology combinations. Absolute reductions range from 0.0959 to 0.3480. All 18 primary endpoint contrasts are significant for both metrics after Holm correction, adjusted p ≤ 2.30 × 10^-26. nDCG absolute losses range from 0.0977 to 0.3694. Means summarize five gallery samples and one fitted checkpoint per learned condition.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: Contrastive versus classification adaptation

name: Comparison setup
text: Same SwAV initialization, NIH partitions and ResNet-50 backbone

name: Significance statement
text:
SupCon advantages
survive global correction
across all prevalence levels.

name: Evidence note
text: Exceptions: cardiomegaly at 0.5% and 1%. The chart shows the 0.5% endpoint.

SupCon has a higher mean than SwAV-CLS in every one of 12 pathology-prevalence conditions and exceeds it significantly in ten globally corrected planned comparisons. At 0.5%: cardiomegaly 0.0163 versus 0.0133, adjusted p > 0.99; emphysema 0.0335 versus 0.0175, adjusted p = 5.34e-7; pneumothorax 0.0660 versus 0.0446, adjusted p = 3.17e-6. The two cardiomegaly contrasts at 0.5% and 1% do not survive correction. This supports the contrastive adaptation finding in the evaluated design, not a universal superiority claim. Objective-specific checkpoint selection and different effective contrastive batch size limit isolation of the objective alone.

title: Above random, with low absolute precision

name: Text 1
text: Above random, with low absolute precision

text: Leading model at 0.5% prevalence: SwAV-SupCon

name: Pathology 0
text: Cardiomegaly

name: Enrichment label 0
text: Random-ranking enrichment

name: Precision 0
text: Precision@10 = 0.0163

name: Pathology 1
text: Emphysema

name: Enrichment label 1
text: Random-ranking enrichment

name: Precision 1
text: Precision@10 = 0.0335

name: Pathology 2
text: Pneumothorax

name: Enrichment label 2
text: Random-ranking enrichment

name: Precision 2
text: Precision@10 = 0.0660

name: Evidence note
text: Random-ranking P@10 = 0.005. Enrichment alone does not establish clinical usefulness.

The three leading absolute means at 0.5% are 0.0163, 0.0335 and 0.0660. Dividing by 0.005 yields 3.26, 6.70 and 13.20 times random expectation. All evaluated model-pathology conditions remain above random at this endpoint. Enrichment increases between 5% and 0.5% in 17 of 18 combinations, but this is descriptive relative discrimination, not proof of adequate retrieval. The study does not measure diagnostic decisions or clinician workflow. Pneumothorax is a cross-source configuration and cannot be compared as a source-controlled estimate of pathology difficulty.

name: Text 1
text: Absolute loss needs endpoint context

name: Example
text: Pneumothorax example

name: Loss heading
text: Absolute P@10 loss

name: Cls loss
text:
SwAV-CLS
0.2841

name: Supcon loss
text:
SwAV-SupCon
0.3480

name: Evidence note
text: SupCon loses more in absolute terms while retaining higher precision at both endpoints.

The example illustrates the scale effect described in manuscript Section IV-C. SupCon P@10 decreases from 0.4140 to 0.0660, a 0.3480 loss. CLS decreases from 0.3287 to 0.0446, a 0.2841 loss. SupCon therefore loses 0.0639 more but remains higher at both endpoints. A larger absolute loss is not by itself evidence of worse rare-case retrieval. Assess endpoint quality and relative enrichment alongside loss. These are paired model means under the evaluated cross-source pneumothorax configuration.

name: Text 1
text: Limits on interpretation

name: Limit heading 0
text: Training uncertainty

name: Limit text 0
text: One fitted checkpoint per learned condition. Five gallery seeds do not estimate retraining variability.

name: Limit heading 1
text: Source confounding

name: Limit text 1
text: SIIM supplies pneumothorax queries and NIH supplies relevant images. Source and retrieval role remain aligned.

name: Limit heading 2
text: Labels and zero-shot scope

name: Limit text 2
text: Target labels are absent from available fine-tuning annotations. Unrecorded target findings may still be present.

name: Limit heading 3
text: Clinical relevance

name: Limit text 3
text: Binary recorded labels define relevance. No radiologist evaluated clinical similarity or diagnostic benefit.

All conditions use ResNet-50, limiting architecture generalization. Classification and SupCon checkpoints use objective-specific selection criteria. TB was excluded after a source-confounding audit, narrowing pathology coverage. No source-separability diagnostic was performed for pneumothorax. NIH labels are report-derived and noisy. External common-class labels are not exhaustive. SIIM metadata do not establish patient uniqueness. Horizontal flipping may affect laterality-dependent findings. The lowest prevalence still provides 100 relevant images, and much larger approximate indexes or lower absolute counts remain untested.

Source: Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx, supplied manuscript. Reference numbers follow the paper.

name: Text 1
text: Conclusions and next experiments

name: Main conclusion
text:
Gallery prevalence belongs in
the retrieval benchmark.

name: Conclusion evidence
text:
Precision and ranking quality decline across every evaluated
model–pathology pair as the target share falls.

name: Adaptation conclusion
text:
Contrastive adaptation leads in this study, with a significant
advantage over SwAV-CLS in 10 of 12 conditions.

name: Next work label
text: Next experiments

name: Next work text
text:
Independent training runs, stronger source controls,
lower relevant-case counts and clinician-assessed relevance.

The paper recommends reporting performance at at least two clinically relevant gallery-prevalence levels. The study shows substantial absolute degradation and pathology-dependent model separation. It supports the evaluated SupCon-versus-classification adaptation result but not an architecture-independent or universal learning-paradigm ordering. Future work should replicate training, broaden architectures, test lower relevant-case counts and improve clinical and source controls.
